8cbd994b4dc46c0e: KATHMANDU: Rescuers recovered the bodies on Friday of two Japanese climbers missing for over a week on a remote Himalayan mountain, an expedition organiser said.

Kumar Chhetri of Cosmo Adventure, which offered the climbers logistical support, said the search began after they failed to return to basecamp on Oct 18 as planned.

Nepal sits in the Himalayas, and its mountains – which include Everest, the world's tallest – have long drawn climbers from across the world.

b07dc07d2b55e28a: ROME, Oct 23 — From blockaded schools in Rome to tent camps in Madrid and street protests in France, young people across Europe are turning their anger on a political class they say is not listening.
Their demands vary, but they are united in wanting to make their often marginalised voices heard, sometimes even with radical methods in the face of heavy-handed policing.

“We are fighting and taking our future in our hands,” said Damiano Fusa, 18, a student at Rome’s Cavour high school, the first to be occupied in a wave of student takeovers that has spread across the Italian capital.

“We’re not represented by anyone,” Fusa told AFP, criticising both Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s hard-right coalition and previous centre-left governments for cutting education funding and ignoring young people’s needs.
Hundreds of thousands of high school and university students have rallied in France, Italy, Spain and other European countries in recent weeks, with some protests descending into violence.

Governments have largely focused on restoring order, with France imposing partial curfews and Italy deploying soldiers, responses protesters say obscure their demands and could make things even worse.
“Politicians are responding in ways that are completely disconnected from reality, completely absurd,” said Luis Marques, a 19-year-old psychology student in Lisbon.
Students are demanding action on soaring rents, more spending on education instead of defence and more job opportunities for young people.
But experts say the unrest reflects a broader sense among many young Europeans that they have been shut out of politics and sidelined.

“These young people do not just feel like they do not have a place in politics, they feel they are not being heard at all,” said Geoffrey Pleyers, president of the International Sociological Association.
Rosario Forlenza, a professor at Rome’s Luiss University, called it a “European generational revolt” rooted in a social and economic crisis “to which politicians cannot give a substantive response”.
“Young people are a minority of the population that is shrinking and so their social, economic, cultural, political and electoral weight is becoming ever more irrelevant,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A person reads messages displayed on a tarp in a camp set to protest against evictions and the housing crisis in Puerta del Sol square in Madrid October 20, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Inspiring other people’
The anger has been particularly palpable in France and Italy, where fresh demonstrations are planned for tomorrow.

“People are very angry, they’ve had enough. Working hard all day and still not being able to fill up their shopping cart,” a 20-year-old student who gave his name as Eddy told AFP at a protest in Bordeaux last weekend.

“Will smashing everything change anything? I think it can be a jolt to wake up the politicians. We don’t know what else to do to make ourselves heard. The ballot box? We don’t believe in it anymore,” he said.
Protest movements across Europe are increasingly drawing inspiration from one another, and even looking to youth-led movements further afield in places like Bangladesh, India and Nepal.
In Italy, one student slogan last week urged protesters to “do as in France”, while shared symbols, including the Jolly Roger pirate flag, have become common across youth rallies.
Marcos Navarro, 22, a laboratory quality-control technician from Madrid, said protesters across Europe were meeting to share tactics.

“They’ve come to ask us: ‘How did you do it? How do you organise yourselves?’ We’ve already exchanged ideas,” said Navarro, who has been camping with hundreds of others in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September to protest housing costs and evictions.
Ayla Herrero, a 26-year-old anthropologist helping at the camp’s infirmary, said it was “inspiring for us to know that we’re inspiring other people, that it doesn’t just stay here”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Protesters lie on the ground and shout slogans during a protest against housing shortage, soaring rents and low wages at Rossio square in Lisbon October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Not acceptable’
Concern about the rise in military spending in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine has also been a rallying point.
Nikos Mavroudis, a 17-year-old high school student in Athens’ Exarchia neighbourhood, said the money could be better spent on his school, where chunks of plaster are falling.
“It’s not acceptable for classrooms to be dangerous,” said Mavroudis, who hopes to become a cook and plans to move elsewhere in Europe to “countries where things are better”.
At Rome’s occupied Morgagni high school, where students have barricaded entrances with desks, protesters pointed to the crumbling infrastructure as evidence of neglect.
An 18-year-old, who did not want to be named, said the media and politicians in Italy were focusing too heavily on looting and vandalism by some protesters.
“It turns hatred against the students who are victims of this system,” he said.
Asked about the violence, Sabrina Brizzola, 24, coordinator of the Italian University Students’ Union, said organisations like hers should “organise and channel this generational rage”.
“We have shared concerns, even if our ways of protesting differ,” she said. — AFP
aea623b03e05139f: CAPE TOWN, Oct 23 — South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books since February 2025 using artificial intelligence, a process she passionately defends despite criticism and threats.
“Grifter”, “villain” — insults abound on social media to describe the author who, in her forties, has become the symbol of AI’s arrival in publishing.
Coral Hart — a pseudonym she uses to protect her real name — told AFP in an interview she had received “tens of thousands” of hate messages and several death threats.
In this hostile environment, few authors using AI agree to speak publicly and show their faces.
“I chose to be the one to step up and say, these are conversations we need to start having,” Hart said.
“This is here... They’re not going to switch it off or unplug it because a bunch of authors said so.”
Before she started writing with AI around 20 months ago, Hart had been working in publishing for 14 years and written several dozen works without the technology.
It took her three months to familiarise herself with the various AI models and build a framework capable of producing a book.

Now she juggles between ChatGPT, which is “really good at dialogue, terrible at prose”; Claude, “really good story structure, terrible at sex drives”; and others like Grok, “completely unhinged” but good on “spicy scenes”.
“If you say, ChatGPT, write me a book, or, Claude, write me a book, you’re going to get a flaming dumpster fire of trash back because it doesn’t have anything (to work with),” Hart said.
The author defines the story concept, a style, details of the characters, and chapter outlines. And only then will her system generate the books.
Hart said when she started, “we could write one paragraph at a time. I usually took two or three prompts to do that.”
“I can now draft the whole book in one sequence.”
Since last year, AI models have “improved vastly”, Hart said. “The prose has improved. The syntax has improved. The sentence structure has improved.”
‘Books are selling’
The first draft of a book is generally not good, the writer said.

It is run through AI for “developmental edits” and then again “to fix any continuity issues, story issues, flat middles, character arcs that are incomplete, plot threads that have been dropped, people whose eye colour has changed.”
At the end of this process, a human proofreader reads through the text to fix any “AI tells that have slipped through” and do some rewriting. “And it’s usually ready to go.”
Although one of her novels made it into Amazon’s top 100 bestsellers, the vast majority of her 371 titles — many of them romance — are tailored to certain readers based on rigorous market research.
She has sold more than one million books, by her own estimate, in digital, print and audio formats, earning more than US$1 million (RM4.08 million) so far this year.
The South African now heads an operation that has trained several hundred people in her method and is preparing to launch software for AI authors called Authorythm.
As for her own production, she mentions her use of AI only when required by a sales platform.
“For the last 16 years, nobody’s asked me what my creative process was,” said Hart, who publishes under more than 10 other pen names.
Now, she was ready to make it public “for the right reasons”.
Regularly accused of contributing to “AI slop” — low-quality AI-generated content in text, video, music, or images — Hart points to the ultimate yardstick: “Books are selling.”
“Readers don’t read rubbish books; they return them,” she said.

The writer has followed the debate around a novel by Haitian-Canadian Thelyson Orelien that was withdrawn from the shortlist for France’s Goncourt prize after accusations that he used AI, which his publisher confirmed on Wednesday.
Critics had praised the book and sales were strong before the controversy, she said, asking: “If you need an AI label to hate something, do you hate it, or do you hate AI?” — AFP
f7d38ec461425fb6: STOCKHOLM, Oct 23 — Bubbles rise through the murky green water as divers tenderly explore a rare 15th-century shipwreck off Stockholm’s coast, believed to be the oldest warship found off Sweden.

“It’s a very big ship, it was around 40-45 metres when it sailed probably,” project leader and marine archaeologist Hakan Altrock from Sweden’s Museum of Wrecks said, overseeing the dives down to the skeletal remains of what is known as Vrak 5, or Shipwreck 5, on a cool October day.
Located off Haringe Castle south of Stockholm, the vessel is thought to be the oldest warship found off Sweden or Denmark, which were joined in a union with Norway in the 15th century.
First discovered in the late 1800s, the shipwreck is one of five lying on the seabed in the Landfjarden sound, most of which have been dated to the 1600s and 1700s.
But in February 2025, researchers were able to date Vrak 5 to the 1480s, or possibly even the 1460s.
“It’s not possible to say if it is Swedish, it could also be Danish,” Altrock said, noting that the timber used to build it comes from the area that is now southeastern Sweden.
“This is the first example of a ship in the Baltic that has been built with the carvel technique... in Scandinavia that we know of,” he said.

He was referring to the boat-building technique where hull planks are laid edge-to-edge rather than overlapping, which made it possible to build bigger and sturdier vessels — necessary with the advent of heavy cannons on ships.
Marine archaeologists excavated the wreck this week in order to better document it, find out more about how it was built, and as part of a special project about food on board.
Among other things, they used special pumps to vacuum up sediment and expose parts of the construction.
Divers found bricks that suggested they had found the galley, in addition to parts of the ship’s rigging.
Matilda Jarl, a PhD student in marine archaeology also at the site, said the crew would have eaten fish, meat and porridge on board.
“A lot of the food would be boiled. So there would be a lot of pottage, which is basically anything that is cooked in a pot,” she said.

“With the food they would also drink beer. The people with a higher status on board would be drinking wine also, but the general crew would be drinking beer instead of water as it kept better,” she added.
It is not yet known why the ship sank where it did.
Altrock said rumours from when the wreck was found in the 19th century referred to a fire on board.
“Perhaps it was sunk when they (the Danes) attacked the Haringe Castle behind us in 1501,” he said. “That’s one theory.”
“Maybe we’ll find traces of where it burned. We’ll see.” — AFP
85a9732fc2b8d940: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — Six in 10 international travellers say travel advertisements look similar and half cannot remember the last tourism ad they saw, according to a report by global tourism platform TOURISE and LIONS Advisory.

The report, IDEAS That Travel, found that tourism brands are competing for attention in a more fragmented environment shaped by social media and artificial intelligence (AI), even as travel demand rises, TOURISE said in a statement.

It is based on an online survey of 8,374 consumers in 13 markets who had travelled internationally in the previous 12 months, conducted in December 2025, and interviews with industry leaders, including Capital A chief executive officer and AirAsia co-founder, Tony Fernandes.

“Travellers are discovering destinations earlier and through more channels than ever, from social feeds and creators to communities and AI tools. That raises the bar for tourism brands,” said Saudi Arabia’s Minister of Tourism, Ahmed Al Khateeb, who is also chairman of TOURISE.

The report found that 39 per cent of travellers expect to travel more in the next 12 months than in 2025, rising to 51 per cent of Gen Z and 47 per cent of millennials. However, 43 per cent find it difficult to tell travel brands apart.
At the same time, it also found that 55 per cent of travellers already use AI to plan holidays, and 62 per cent expect to use it more over the next year.

Global travel and transport advertising spending rebounded to an estimated US$32.4 billion (RM132 billion) in 2025, but the category’s share of total advertising remains below pre-pandemic levels. Restoring it to three per cent would require spending to reach US$43.4 billion by 2027, the report said.

It recommends smarter investment in social media, creator, video and entertainment channels rather than simply more spending, and sets out a framework built on five factors: investment, distinctiveness, engagement, authenticity and seamlessness. — Bernama

345cf4df6686d5a3: SHAH ALAM: A series of accidents involving heavy vehicles, including a 12-vehicle pile-up that injured four people earlier this month, has renewed calls for urgent safety improvements along Persiaran Mokhtar Dahari.
More than 100 residents from Alam Budiman and neighbouring housing areas staged a protest at the Jalan Alam Budiman traffic junction today, highlighting what they described as a "killer road".

Carrying a replica coffin and placing mock graves at the intersection, they called on the authorities to address recurring accidents and expedite a proposed 5km flyover project, which they said had been mooted 15 years ago.

Gabungan Penduduk U10 residents' association chairman Badrul Hisham Shahbudin said the proposed flyover was needed to accommodate growing traffic volumes and improve safety for motorists from Puncak Alam, Puncak Perdana, Meru, Saujana Utama and surrounding areas.
"We hope the proposed flyover will be given serious attention as this is a main route for motorists from these areas to access Dash.

"We have been calling for road widening and the construction of a flyover for years because we believe these are the solutions needed. However, we still want to know when the project will be implemented," he said after the protest.
Greenhill Residence chairman Mohd Zailani Johari, 57, called for immediate safety measures rather than leaving residents to wait for the proposed flyover.
He said the recent accidents involving heavy vehicles had heightened fear and trauma among residents.
"Residents want safety measures to be implemented immediately because we cannot simply wait for the flyover to be built while road users continue to face risks every day.
"We hope the authorities will review the road conditions and introduce improvements in the near future," he said.

Their protest follows a series of crashes along the route this month, including an incident on Oct 9 in which a lorry crashed into 11 other vehicles at the Alam Budiman traffic lights, injuring four people.
Two victims, a man and a woman, suffered serious head injuries, while two other men sustained minor injuries.
Police later confirmed that the 51-year-old lorry driver had tested positive for amphetamine and methamphetamine.
Based on preliminary investigations, the driver claimed that his vehicle suffered brake failure while travelling downhill from Puncak Perdana towards Puncak Alam, causing him to lose control.
On Oct 16, another accident involving several vehicles occurred at Kilometre 9.2 of Persiaran Mokhtar Dahari.
A four-wheel-drive vehicle reportedly hit the rear of a lorry before its driver lost control and veered into the opposite lane, colliding with another lorry and a car.
Three days later, a lorry carrying gravel overturned near the entrance to the Alam Budiman business centre after its driver reportedly lost control while travelling downhill.
The driver was trapped in the wreckage before being rescued.

On Oct 21, the Selangor Public Works Department announced plans to add a 300m lane from Puncak Alam towards Shah Alam at the Alam Budiman junction, alongside additional street lighting, traffic light upgrades and other safety improvements.
Preliminary works were under way, with physical construction expected to begin in mid-2027, according to a report published on Oct 22.
The proposed improvements are aimed at easing congestion and improving safety along the route, which serves several rapidly growing residential areas.

eea3ae9ab75546af: PUTRAJAYA: The Federal Court has clarified the application of a statutory presumption of knowledge in drug-trafficking cases, ruling that it can apply when drugs are found inside a bag under an accused’s custody and control.

The decision came as a three-member bench chaired by Justice Abu Bakar Jais, with Justices Ruzima Ghazali and Azimah Omar, dismissed the appeal by former lorry driver Ahmad Fahmi Hasnu against his conviction for trafficking 1.46kg of methamphetamine, commonly known as syabu.

In delivering the judgment, Ruzima said the central issue was whether Section 37(d) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 could be invoked when the drugs were found in a bag inside a car used by the accused.

Fahmi argued that a car was not a “container” within the meaning of the provision and that the prosecution had to prove his knowledge of the drugs through evidence rather than rely on a statutory presumption.
However, the Federal Court found that the drugs were inside a black backpack on the rear seat of the Perodua Myvi he was using.
Police officers had seen him opening the rear door and reaching towards the bag when they approached him during an operation in Seri Kembangan.

The distinction is legally significant as the court's reasoning focused on the bag containing the drugs and the accused’s custody and control of it, rather than treating the mere presence of drugs somewhere in a vehicle as sufficient to invoke the presumption.
Section 37(d) provides that a person who has custody or control of anything containing dangerous drugs is presumed to possess the drugs and knows their nature, unless the contrary is proved.
Fahmi, 39, claimed the bag might have belonged to his brother-in-law or the latter's friend. The courts found that he had failed to rebut the presumption.

The Federal Court upheld the conviction and the 30-year prison sentence imposed by the High Court and affirmed by the Court of Appeal. Fahmi was also ordered to receive 12 strokes of the rotan, the minimum punishment applicable to him as he is below 50.
He was convicted of trafficking 1,464.5g of methamphetamine at an apartment in Taman Pinggiran Putra, Seri Kembangan, at about 6.45pm on Oct 8, 2020.
Deputy public prosecutor Zain Ibrahim appeared for the prosecution, while Affifuddin Ahmad Hafifi and Aina Melina Johan Ariff represented Fahmi.

bc377e4efe2ee531: KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysian Media Council (MMC) wants media organisations to refrain from publishing details or unverified social media content that could directly or indirectly identify children involved in incidents as suspects, victims or witnesses.

In a statement, it reminded newsrooms that under Clause 9.3 of its Code of Conduct, the interests of children under 18 must be protected and may only be overridden where there is an exceptional public benefit.
"Information that attracts public attention does not necessarily serve the public interest," it said.

MMC acknowledged that incidents involving minors, particularly in schools, were matters of legitimate public concern. However, it said, it must be balanced against the potential harm to the children involved.
Under Clause 4.3, the names, photographs and identifiable locations of juvenile suspects or persons of interest must not be published or broadcast, it said.
MMC also cautioned that details such as a child's age, class, family background and social media accounts could indirectly reveal their identity.

"Materials circulating on social media and messaging platforms, including personal notes, messages, screenshots, photographs and videos allegedly involving or originating from a minor, must not be presented as established facts without appropriate verification of their source and authenticity," MMC said.

It added that under Clause 1.6, unverified information may only be reported where there is a clear public benefit, reasonable attempts at verification have been made, and the information is clearly identified as unverified.
"Such reporting must not be accompanied by speculation or misleading conclusions," it said.
MMC urged newsrooms to respect the presumption of innocence, avoid sensationalism, show compassion when interviewing affected families, and review and correct past coverage that breached the Code.
Members of the public affected by media coverage that may have breached the Code can lodge complaints through MMC's Grievance Mechanism.
15ad9d2caf8d88e3: PARIS: France will deploy some 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests this weekend after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, the government said Friday.

President Emmanuel Macron, who according to aides is postponing a visit later this month to Nigeria and Senegal amid the crisis, held a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and was to meet security forces.

He was also set to host for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked the movement that has broadened into a nationwide show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.

Some 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, interior minister Laurent Nunez said at a press conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.

The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.

Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.
Nunez was expected to visit the city Friday to "inspect the security arrangements" at the request of the prime minister's office, it said.

At Macron's meeting with students, "We will present our demands to him – which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system," Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal) told AFP.
Macron's government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last Saturday.
In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, justice minister Gerald Darmanin said.
On Thursday, Macron called for "the utmost severity" against "acts of delinquency", accusing "ultra-left" groups of having sought to "bring down the republic" last weekend.
'Police have a responsibility'
On Saturday, a second round of demonstrations is expected across France.
Lyon's city centre in the southeast will be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.

Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an "exceptional basis" – the only one authorised in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department.

They also reversed a decision to suspend all public transport in the city on Saturday. But in the capital, leading museums, including the Louvre, will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.
Some 20% more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend after heavy criticism of the anticipation and intelligence gathering of police last week.

"In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government's debt pile also troubling investors.
A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.
It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off, where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70% of the vote.

e6058ffa0a6e8798: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises

Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?

In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
—Jessica Hamzelou
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science.
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

—Software developer Ian Landsman says on X that volunteer Ondřej Surý’s work on patching PHP vulnerabilities makes him an unsung hero of the entire internet.
One more thing
STUART BRADFORD
How sounds can turn us on to the wonders of the universe
For decades, astronomy has relied on visual information to make sense of the cosmos: images, charts, and graphs. Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe.

Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education.
Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing.

334763a1c12bbad1: PARIS, Oct 23 — In a fresh hammer blow for Kenyan athletics, world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended for doping, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced today.
The highly decorated 33-year-old Kenyan, who won Olympic gold in the Covid-delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, was suspended after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for banned blood booster EPO.
An athlete is provisionally suspended while the case is investigated.
Jepchirchir joins more than 140 Kenyan athletes, including current women’s marathon world record-holder Ruth Chepngetich, who have been suspended or banned by the AIU since 2017.
The AIU said Jepchirchir’s out-of-competition sample had been collected in Kenya prior to her recent Sydney Marathon victory.

Jepchirchir’s lauded career has also seen her as a former world record-holder in the half-marathon while she is a four-time World Marathon Major winner having captured the Sydney Marathon (2026), the London Marathon (2024), the Boston Marathon (2022) and the New York Marathon (2021).
The decision of World Athletics to award Nairobi the 2029 world championships is likely to increase the scrutiny of the east African nation’s anti-doping policies. — AFP

9a07f76d91ad29f9: PUTRAJAYA: The Federal Court today upheld the 30-year jail term and 12 strokes of the rotan imposed on a former lorry driver for trafficking 1.4645 kilogrammes (kg) of methamphetamine.

A three-judge panel led by Court of Appeal President Datuk Seri Abu Bakar Jais, together with Federal Court judges Datuk Che Mohd Ruzima Ghazali and Datuk Azimah Omar, dismissed Ahmad Fahmi Mohd Hasnu's appeal against his conviction and sentence.

Delivering the court's unanimous decision, Che Mohd Ruzima said the High Court judge had correctly applied the presumption of knowledge under Section 37(d) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, and that the appellant (Fahmi) had failed to rebut the presumption.

"We find that the drugs were inside a bag, and the bag was in the possession and control of the appellant," he said, adding that the court rejected the defence's argument that the drugs had been found inside the car.

Che Mohd Ruzima said the court found that the drugs had not been discovered concealed in any part of the car driven by the appellant, but were found inside a bag on the right rear seat of the vehicle.

He said the court also gave weight to several key facts - the appellant was driving the car alone at the time of the incident, the bag was in a clearly visible location, and he was seen moving towards and reaching for the bag when the raid was conducted.
"Therefore, there is no reason for us to amend the conviction from trafficking to possession, as proposed by the appellant.
The appeal is dismissed, and the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court and upheld by the Court of Appeal are maintained," he said.

The defence had argued that the High Court judge erred in invoking the presumption of knowledge under Section 37(d), contending that the presumption could not be applied to drugs found inside a vehicle because a vehicle did not fall within the definition of "anything whatsoever containing".

On May 13, 2024, the High Court found Fahmi, 39, guilty of trafficking 1.4645 kg of methamphetamine at the Rusella apartment complex in Taman Pinggiran Putra, Seri Kembangan, Selangor, at 6.45 pm on Oct 8, 2020.
On March 24 last year, the Court of Appeal dismissed Ahmad Fahmi's appeal and upheld the High Court's decision.
At today's proceedings, Ahmad Fahmi was represented by lawyer Afifuddin Ahmad Hafifi, while Deputy Public Prosecutor Mohd Zain Ibrahim appeared for the prosecution.

“Oil is at five-month highs amid speculation there may be renewed US-Israeli strikes after next month’s US midterm elections.

“Escalating tensions in Ukraine and the prospect of increased energy demand as the northern hemisphere heads into the winter months are only adding to the upwards pressure on oil and gas prices,” Hewson added.

77b98a1fcc32d5af: SYDNEY: Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about US$2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.
From Singapore and Shanghai to London and Berlin, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days.

Competitors such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones.
It is also an early challenge for Apple's new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.

Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary".
Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online.
In Sydney, which was the first Apple store to sell the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).

"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 (US$2,734) for a 512GB Duo.

In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to six straight quarters of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices.
Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi, but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6am for Apple's first foldable.
"I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.
Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models.
Others were resellers.

In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 (US$2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked.
Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain.
"Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said.
Mixed reviews

Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.
But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers.
They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple customers.

"It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber.

Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the US$2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone."
In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one.

"I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices."
TOUGH TO FIND
Apple's entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC.
IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.
"Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo.
"Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said.
cd571cf310208a77: KUALA LUMPUR: A little reassurance from Lai Pei Jing is helping Hoo Pang Ron break new ground on the badminton court.
Pang Ron credited his partner's trust after they reached the French Open semi-finals on Friday, marking his first consecutive last-four appearances.
The world No. 31 overcame Germany's world No. 27 Marvin Seidel–Thuc Phuong Nguyen 21–17, 20–22, 21–18 in their quarter-final at Arena Grand Paris.
"She gave me more confidence and asked me to do whatever I wanted to do, and she would follow me," said Pang Ron in a post-match interview.
"Even when I played some shots wrongly, she said it was okay and that we could still do it."
That encouragement helped the independent pair fight back from a narrow second-game defeat and keep their title bid alive.
The result built on their Denmark Open semi-final appearance last week, giving Pang Ron a personal milestone.
"I'm really happy. This is our first time reaching consecutive semi-finals. I've never done this in my career before, so thanks to my partner," he said.
"But we have to keep focusing on the next match."
Their progress in Paris has demanded persistence, with all three victories going the distance.
Pang Ron–Pei Jing opened by recovering from a game down to beat China's Gao Jia Xuan–Wu Meng Ying 14–21, 21–15, 21–15.
They then battled past Taiwan's Liu Kuang Heng–Hsu Yin Hui 21–13, 13–21, 21–17 on Thursday.
Seidel–Nguyen presented another test after eliminating Malaysia's Goh Soon Huat–Shevon Lai and China's second seeds Jiang Zhen Bang–Wei Ya Xin in the opening two rounds.
With the margins tight again, Pei Jing said they focused on their strategy, and the next shot helped them stay on course.
"It was really point for point throughout the match. We were trying to focus on every single shot, what we had to do and our strategy," she said.
Pang Ron–Pei Jing will face China's sixth seeds Guo Xin Wa–Cheng Fang Hui next for a place in the final.
2b5637aeef0bde89: KOTA BARU: Perikatan Nasional (PN) had invited Bersatu to attend a supreme council meeting as early as Sept 20, but it was postponed due to a commitment involving the coalition chairman, said Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin.

The Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan) president said the invitation, extended after the High Court granted a stay on the suspension and deregistration of PN, was not the first time the coalition had invited Bersatu to the meeting.
Hamzah said Bersatu had the right to attend the meeting if they wished to do so.

"This is not the first time PN has invited Bersatu to a meeting. The first invitation was issued on Sept 20, but the meeting was postponed because the chairman had other commitments," he told reporters.
The invitation comes amid an internal dispute that threatened PN's status as a registered political coalition.

The dispute began after Bersatu lodged a complaint with the Registrar of Societies (RoS), alleging that it had been excluded from a PN Supreme Council meeting on July 16. The party also questioned its membership status within the coalition.
RoS confirmed receiving the complaint on Aug 11 before issuing a show-cause notice to PN on Sept 22, requiring it to explain why its registration should not be cancelled.
The following day, RoS suspended PN's activities under subsection 13(2A) of the Societies Act 1966.
On Oct 20, RoS cancelled PN's registration under subparagraph 13(1)(c)(iv) of the same Act.
Hamzah said PN had previously taken similar action against Parti Rakyat India Malaysia (MIPP) after receiving complaints about internal problems within the party.
He said a letter had been sent to MIPP asking it to resolve the issues, adding that the party would not be invited to meetings until they were settled.
"Before the meeting even started, MIPP had already said it received a letter. The same thing happened to Bersatu.
"If I were the secretary-general, I would do the same thing," he said.
Hamzah said PN secretary-general Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan, a lawyer, was expected to act in accordance with the law and regulations.
He said Takiyuddin should not be blamed for carrying out his duties according to the rules.
"He is a lawyer, so his job is to follow the law and regulations. This should be accepted positively," he said.
Yesterday, Takiyuddin said the coalition would convene a meeting soon following the High Court's decision to grant a stay on the RoS action.
7a6b8de95a5b8efd: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 23 — The Malaysian Highway Authority (LLM) and Prosignal Consortium Sdn Bhd have been asked to provide a detailed explanation of problems affecting users of the local navigation app TuJu, including their causes, technical issues and corrective measures.

5bd5bb41c0278f43: PETALING JAYA: Isi rumah di Malaysia berbelanja lebih banyak untuk makan di luar pada 2024, dengan purata RM902.70 sebulan diperuntukkan untuk makan di luar, berbanding RM875.80 untuk makanan di rumah, menurut Institut Penyelidikan Khazanah (KRI).

Laporan 'The State of Households 2026' oleh KRI menyatakan, trend ini dikenal pasti di tengah-tengah kebimbangan yang kian meningkat mengenai tahap kesihatan rakyat, dengan lebih separuh daripada orang dewasa di Malaysia dikategorikan sebagai mempunyai berat badan berlebihan atau obes pada 2023.

Perbelanjaan isi rumah untuk makan di luar meningkat merentasi semua kumpulan pendapatan antara 2019 dan 2024, namun lonjakan itu lebih ketara dalam kalangan 80% isi rumah terbawah (B80), dengan purata perbelanjaan meningkat hampir 1.5 kali ganda sepanjang tempoh lima tahun tersebut.
Bagi 20% isi rumah teratas (T20), perbelanjaan untuk makan di luar mencatatkan peningkatan kurang daripada 1.3 kali ganda.
“Faktor yang mungkin mendorong peningkatan berterusan dalam perbelanjaan makan di luar ini termasuk kos sara hidup yang lebih tinggi serta perubahan gaya hidup,” menurut laporan itu.

“Perkembangan ini berisiko memberi implikasi terhadap kesihatan awam memandangkan tabiat makan di luar sering dikaitkan dengan kualiti diet yang rendah, yang seterusnya meningkatkan risiko obesiti dan penyakit tidak berjangkit (NCD).”
Laporan itu turut mendedahkan bahawa bahagian populasi yang tergolong dalam kategori berat badan berlebihan dan obes, faktor risiko utama bagi NCD, meningkat antara 2019 dan 2023.
Pada 2023, sebanyak 32.6% orang dewasa di Malaysia mengalami berat badan berlebihan manakala 21.8% lagi obes, bermakna lebih separuh daripada populasi dewasa (54.4%) melebihi julat berat badan sihat.

Laporan itu turut menekankan beberapa trend kesihatan membimbangkan yang lain, termasuk penurunan tahap aktiviti fizikal antara 2019 dan 2023, terutamanya di kawasan bandar, di mana jenis pekerjaan, pilihan pengangkutan, gaya hidup dan persekitaran tempat tinggal mungkin mempengaruhi tahap keaktifan.
Sebahagian besar rakyat Malaysia juga gagal memenuhi saranan pengambilan buah-buahan dan sayur-sayuran pada 2023, tambahnya.
Sementara itu, diabetes muncul sebagai antara lima punca utama kematian di kebanyakan negeri antara 2022 dan 2024.
9183a63d28f18289: LONDON: Prince Harry's wife Meghan said Friday she was "deeply distressed" following accusations her father had possessed images of child abuse, adding she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous "troubling and disturbing" allegations.
The Sun, Daily Mail and Telegraph newspapers reported Friday that images had allegedly been found among her father Thomas Markle's possessions at his former home in the Philippines.
After the reports, Meghan revealed that in 2018 she had seen a letter sent to London's Metropolitan Police making similar accusations.
"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said in a statement.

Harry, the second son of King Charles III and estranged brother of heir to the throne Prince William, married the former American actress at the royal family's Windsor Castle estate in May 2018. Thomas Markle did not attend.
"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said in the statement.

Meghan, who has two children with Harry – Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five – said she hoped it could "now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them."
The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud.
But the family made an unexpected return to live in the United Kingdom in August.

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children," Meghan added.
a3ee59efa61af645: KAJANG: Police have ruled out foul play in a helium tank explosion that killed a 49-year-old worker at a scrap metal processing factory in Sungai Chua here today.

“They are taking the initiative to improve their livelihoods, raise their household incomes, and secure a better future for their children.
“Their efforts should be appreciated, encouraged and supported, not jeopardised by the absence of formal land documentation.”

On Sunday, the association's president, Napolean Ningkos, said the EUDR, which will kick in next year, could threaten the income of smallholders, who are not able to produce the required land documentation, mapping and geolocation data.

Nanta welcomed an earlier commitment by the state's food industry, commodity and regional development minister, Dr Stephen Rundi Utom, to work with the federal plantation and commodities ministry and the Malaysian palm oil certification council in seeking a special exemption from the EU for NCR land under the EUDR.

“One should not be pursued at the expense of the other,” he said.

6e74b58a109f42d1: SINGAPORE, Oct 23 — Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and Bank of Thailand (BOT) have joined the Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency (BLOOM) initiative as policymaker members, said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) today.

MAS said that through the initiative, all three central banks will partner with industry players across their respective jurisdictions to develop common approaches for cross-border use of digital money.
It covers how different forms of digital money can be accepted, exchanged and settled across institutions, networks and jurisdictions.

“BLOOM is a public-private initiative that brings together policymakers, financial institutions, payment networks and technology providers to advance the use of digital money in cross-border financial activity,” the central bank said in a statement today.
The initiative aims to deepen engagement between policymakers and the industry on settlement infrastructure and frameworks that promote interoperability for cross-border digital money transactions.
It will include how relevant international standards and jurisdiction-specific supervisory expectations can be applied for such transactions, while allowing for differences in local requirements.

“Through the development of implementation frameworks and alignment of commercial and operating arrangements, BLOOM will reduce the need for financial institutions to establish separate arrangements with each counterparty or market, lowering implementation cost and improving time to market.
“At the same time, the participation of central banks will ensure that public policy and regulatory considerations are taken into account as these approaches are developed,” said MAS.
BLOOM’s participation has expanded to include Airwallex, Mastercard, Maybank, Monee, Nium, Ripple, ShopeePay, Visa and the World Bank Group.

Existing participants include Anchorage Digital, Ant International, Circle, Coinbase, DBS, JP Morgan, Kasikornbank, OCBC, Partior, Schroders, Standard Chartered, StraitsX, Stripe, Temasek, UOB and Xweave.

“Together, the participants are advancing digital money applications across payments, treasury and trade finance, including the use of tokenised deposits, regulated stablecoins and settlement across payment networks.

“The World Bank Group’s participation as a multilateral development bank provides an opportunity to contribute its global experience in payment systems modernisation, cross-border payments, and financial inclusion,” said MAS. — Bernama
ff55915616e3a5c5: Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I.

Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as "Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop." In the podcast Pivot to AI, podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: "This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI."

I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous.

I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse, which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place.

Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them.

All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful.

Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today.

In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception.

Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to "deprecate the Assisted-by Tag." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code submissions.

That doesn't mean you can turn in slop, though. That code won't pass muster. As Torvalds told me in a note the other day: "I think the whole 'don't use AI for commit messages' kind of argument … Maybe it's well-intentioned, but I think it's entirely misguided. I really think we want competent people to use AI as a tool."

Competent is the key word there. Torvalds also wrote: "The 'clueless people using AI' problem is different. I do think we want to discourage that. Not discourage the people who use AI and truly want to learn and truly want to become useful members of the kernel community – but discourage the drive-by patches, and discourage people who just want to feel like they sent a patch and never really wanted to become anything more. We all start clueless, but some people spend the time and effort to become something more." Exactly so.

As Torvalds said at Open Source Summit Europe: "I think [vibe-coding is] a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with." He added: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug" to programming.

Besides, AI has already proven very useful for improving Linux code. As long-term Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman told me back in March: "Months ago, we were getting what we called 'AI slop,' AI-generated security reports that were obviously wrong or low quality." But then, "something happened a month ago, and the world switched. Now we have real reports." It's not just Linux, he continued. "All open source projects have real reports that are made with AI, but they're good, and they're real."

True, the maintainers are getting buried in good bug reports now, but as Kroah-Hartman and discussed in Prague, AI bug finders might eventually exhaust the readily discoverable problems, easing the pressure on maintainers.

Another AI win is that you can use AI to reverse-engineer Windows drivers for Linux more easily. Christian F.K. Schaller, Red Hat's director of software engineering, created hw-harness while working on a Linux driver for a slide scanner. This open source project provides "tooling for working out how a piece of hardware behaves so that you can write a Linux driver for it."

By automating some seriously slow, tedious ways of figuring out what a binary-only driver was doing with the hardware, Schaller has made building Linux drivers from Windows drivers much easier. I know, because I did this myself back in the mid-2000s, and those manual methods are still what people use today. This could go a long way toward fixing one of those lingering annoyances of the Linux desktop: poor or entirely missing hardware drivers.

In the meantime, Torvalds told me: "Well, in all fairness, we do clearly have an 'AI problem.' Or rather, we have two independent AI problems: we have a large codebase that AI finds real bugs in, and that adds a lot of work on already fairly overworked maintainers. And then we have people who use AI to generate patches without actually understanding the code in question."

He continued: "But I'd argue that these aren't problems with AI itself; they are just problems that are exposed by AI. They are very much both very real problems, and I understand that people can really come to dislike – and even hate – AI due to them, but I do think the underlying issue isn't AI itself."
It's how people misuse AI. In the right hands, as the top Linux programmers are showing us, AI can be useful. ®
4d9ebe56a9774973: Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it.

464b3c78cffbc35d: PUTRAJAYA: The Federal Court has tentatively fixed Dec 16 to hear a constitutional challenge by 10 former Negeri Sembilan state executive council members over whether the Yang Dipertuan Besar can revoke their appointments without the menteri besar’s advice.
The date was set by deputy registrar Azaraorni Abd Rahman following a case management session attended by the parties.
However, the hearing may not proceed if the state secretary and state government succeed in their bid to strike out the suit in the Seremban High Court.

Lawyers for the two respondents informed Azaraorni that they intended to challenge the validity of the originating summons, arguing that the 10 former exco members should have initiated their legal action through a judicial review instead.
High Court judge Roz Mawar Rozain is scheduled to hear the application on Nov 16.

The 10 former exco members filed the originating summons in the Seremban High Court on Oct 5 through Messrs Hafarizam Wan & Aisha Mubarak, naming the Negeri Sembilan state secretary and state government as respondents.
They are seeking a declaration that the state gazette revoking their appointments is null and void. They are also seeking damages, including exemplary and aggravated damages.

In a notice of motion filed at the Federal Court on Oct 14, they asked the apex court to determine whether Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir’s revocation of their appointments, which took effect on Sept 20 and was gazetted four days later, was constitutional.

They also want the court to clarify whether the phrase “at the ruler’s pleasure” in the state constitution gives the ruler unrestricted power to revoke their appointments without regard to other constitutional provisions governing the exercise of royal powers.

The 10 former exco members lost their positions after Tuanku Muhriz revoked their appointments following their claims that his removal in April was legitimate and their assertion that Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja'afar had become the new ruler.
The palace regarded their actions as inconsistent with their oath of loyalty to the ruler and the royal institution.
The Federal Court’s determination will depend on whether the originating summons survives the challenge at the High Court.
In today's proceedings, Abdul Rashid Ismail, Siti Nurani Zahidi and Yong Yue Lu appeared for the state secretary, while Marisa Regina Aris Rizal represented the state government.
Norhazira Abu Haiyan acted for the 10 former exco members.

86d3f2c86706447f: Peacock’s series, Crystal Lake, doesn’t feel like a Friday the 13th movie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the original Friday the 13th movie but avoids major Crystal Lake spoilers.)

Instead, Crystal Lake strives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son Jason.

Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans who knew very little about her. 65d4301f9e86d07f: BANGKOK, Oct 23 — Thailand plans to impose mandatory safety standards on electric vehicle (EV) batteries covering their manufacture, import and sale, the government said today, as the country seeks to build confidence in its growing EV industry, Xinhua reported.

The standard applies to non-lead-acid rechargeable batteries in battery-electric passenger and goods vehicles with at least four wheels. It requires protection against overcharging, overheating and short circuits, said deputy government spokesperson Lalida Periswiwatana.

Under a draft ministerial regulation, manufacturers and importers would need licences under Thailand’s Industrial Product Standards Act, while retailers would only sell products that are licensed and meet the standard.

The rules would take effect 180 days after publication in the official Royal Gazette. Businesses are advised to follow the progress of the regulation and prepare for product standards, testing, and licensing requirements, Lalida said in a statement.

Beyond pre-market safety controls, the Ministry of Industry has also been asked to study ways to track batteries after their service life ends. Lalida said the proposal remains under consideration and is not yet a take-back or mandatory recycling scheme.

The government wants Thailand’s EV industry to grow with quality, not just by increasing production capacity or sales, she said, adding that this approach would build consumer confidence, strengthen the competitiveness of the South-east Asian country’s EV industry, and drive the economy alongside sustainable environmental care. — Bernama-Xinhua
9a0af2f9075d0a33: BENGALURU: The combined China-India-Brazil market for weight-loss drugs could grow to US$22 billion by 2035 from US$6.6 billion currently, J.P. Morgan estimated, as improving affordability and broader access drive adoption in largely untapped patient populations.
The addressable market could grow at an annual rate of 15% through 2035, J.P. Morgan analysts led by Yang Huang said in a note on Friday, given the countries' large diabetes and obesity burdens.
GLP-1 drugs, such as Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound, have become some of the most sought-after medicines for weight-loss and diabetes treatment globally.

China and India are home to some of the world's largest diabetes patient populations, accounting for more than 25% and 15% of global diagnosed cases, respectively, while about 12% of Brazilian adults have diabetes, according to J.P. Morgan.
The three countries also face a growing obesity burden. China's overweight and obese population could exceed 65% by 2030, while India's adult obesity rate is projected to reach 11% by 2035.
"GLP-1 is transitioning from a developed-market growth theme to a broader global access story..." the analysts said.
"With patent cliffs, generic launches and policy-engineered price cuts now improving GLP-1 affordability, the three markets are converging on the same destination."
GLP-1's uptake in many emerging markets has remained low due to affordability concerns. Penetration is below 0.1% in China and under 0.2% in India, versus 4%-5% in the US, according to the note.
While Brazil is currently the largest of the three markets, obesity-drug penetration is projected to reach only 7%-8% of its obese population by 2035, compared with about 30% in the US.

J.P. Morgan expects China to overtake Brazil by 2027, with its market reaching US$13.7 billion by 2035, versus US$8 billion for Brazil, supported by its large diabetes burden and wider reimbursement for GLP-1 therapies.

For India, the smallest of the three markets, conservative attitudes toward GLP-1 drugs, alongside affordability concerns, remain key barriers to adoption, J.P. Morgan said, as hesitancy around injectables and slow-shifting cultural attitudes persist.
The brokerage highlighted China's Innovent, Divi's Laboratories and Torrent Pharmaceuticals in India, and Brazil's RD Saude as its key stocks to play the GLP-1 growth theme.

77e8ef5dc307faf3: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 23 — The Federal Court has set December 16 to hear the legal bid filed by ten deposed Negeri Sembilan State Executive Council (Exco) members to challenge the state ruler’s decision last month to revoke their appointments.

Lawyer Datuk Wira Mohd Hafarizam Harun, representing the former exco members, and lawyer Marisa Regina Mohd Aris Rizal, appearing for the Negeri Sembilan government, confirmed the hearing date when contacted by Bernama after case management Deputy Registrar Azaraorni Abd Rahman.

The 10 are Datuk Mohd Faizal Ramli, Datuk Zaifulbahri Idris, Mustapha Nagoor, Siow Kong Choon, Siti Nur Umaira Hasim, Datuk Mohd Asna Amin, Datuk Mohd Razi Mohd Ali, Suhaimizan Bizar, Datuk Mohd Fairuz Mohd Isa and Datuk Razali Abu Samah.
They filed the notice of motion on October 14 and named the Negeri Sembilan State Secretary and the State Government as respondents.

On October 5, they filed an originating summons at the Seremban High Court to challenge the validity of the gazette notification revoking their appointments as members of the Negeri Sembilan State Exco.

One of the questions is whether Article 38(5), when read together with Articles 38(2), 38(3), 38(4), 40(1), 40(1A), and 40(2) of the State Constitution of Negeri Sembilan, authorises the Yang Dipertuan Besar to revoke the appointment of an Exco member without the advice of the Menteri Besar.

Should the answer to that question be in the negative, they seek a determination as to whether the revocation of the Exco appointments, as gazetted on September 24, was carried out in accordance with the State Constitution of Negeri Sembilan, and whether such revocation is null, void, and of no legal effect.

Another question is whether Article 38(5), read together with Article 28(1) of the State Constitution, implies that the term Raja Pemerintah (Ruler) refers to the Yang Dipertuan Besar, vesting him with the authority to revoke the appointment of an Exco member at his own discretion, without the advice of the Menteri Besar.
If the answer to this question is in the negative, then it must be determined whether their dismissal is contrary to the State Constitution.
On September 20, the Negeri Sembilan Palace announced that the Yang Dipertuan Besar, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, had revoked the appointments of the 10 Exco members with immediate effect.
The revocation of their appointments was gazetted on September 24, with their removal taking effect on September 20.

affe2185b1f2b488: Working in the same place for what feels like millennia can have its benefits, however working for the same place for what seems like millennia carrying over all the benefits of your original contract can be even better than that.

What is in play, however, as the PFY has recently discovered, is accumulated sick leave. It appears that we've been racking up two weeks a year to a point that I now have sufficient sick leave to safely get leprosy.
Obviously, I'm not going to exercise that particular option, but both the PFY and I have been considering roads not taken in recent times...
"Ahh... Just, um, following up on your recent, uh, illnesses." The Boss asks uneasily.
"Oh yes?" I ask.
"This, uh, acute bronchitis a few Fridays back."
"Oh yeah, it was terrible," I lie. "Hacking cough, not pleasant at all. I was wheezing like a coal-fired Trabant."
"And that particular illness lasted... a single day?"
"Apparently," I say. "All good now though."
"And Stephen. He had acute... otitis media around the same time."
"The ear thing?" I respond. "Yes, apparently it really affected his balance."
"Okay, fair enough. But then you had acute sinusitis on the Monday? And Stephen had asthma on the Tuesday?"
"Yes, that sounds about right." I nod.
"Then.. Back spasms for you last Friday and campylobacter for Stephen on Monday?"

"I blame myself. I carried a large Vindaloo banquet for six back to work on the Wednesday night. The PFY took the leftovers back home for dinner following day. He's never been great with food hygiene."
"And then I see fibromyalgia for you and food poisoning for Stephen?"
"Yeah, like I said, he's not that great with food hygiene. He tends to follow the five minute rule."
"Hmm. And is there any reason why you seem to be getting sick in... uh... alphabetical order?" the Boss asks.
"It's as much a mystery to you as to me," I admit, making a mental note to vary things a bit. "Illness seems to be attracted to us like a hippy to a salt lamp."
"And, uh, no medical certificate for any of these illnesses?" the Boss enquires.
"I checked with Claude, and he told me that according to my contract I'd only need a med cert for a three-or-more-days illness."
"You have been ill for more than three days. Just yesterday you had conjunctivitis."
"Firstly, I believe it's contiguous sick days, and secondly, the conjunctivitis was so bad it would have been irresponsible to drive to the doctor..."
"And yet your eyesight was sufficient for you to type in questions to Claude?" the Boss asks, astutely.
"Oh no, I spoke to Claude."
It's a bit early to be calling check-mate at this stage, but I have to admit to feeling smug.
"The actual wording of your contract indicates that the conditions can be varied by written notice," the Boss points out.
"And I take it you've written a notice?" I ask, noticing a folded page in the Boss' hand.
The Boss hands the paper to me, still warm from the printer.
"You'll note that it's in writing, signed and dated," the Boss points out.
"Well that's me told," I say, feeling a little like I'll have a dental problem tomorrow.
...two days later...
"And so I'm just after your med cert for your, er, dental abscess," the Boss asks, skipping the niceties.

"Oh yes, right. I spoke to Claude, and he looked over my contract again. Apparently he says that giving me written notice is (a) not retrospective, and that I probably already had the dental issue before you gave me written notice, but also (b) written notice can only vary the contract by mutual agreement."
"And I take it you don't agree?" the Boss asks.
"Claude says I don't. But I got a medical opinion anyway."
… two minutes later..
"An email, apparently from Claude, saying it definitely sounds like you have an abscess is NOT a medical certificate."
"But Claude's a medical expert. He's got access to a vast database of medical information on the web."
"That doesn't count," the Boss snaps.
"Claude says it does," I counter.
"Oh, so Claude's a lawyer as well then?" the Boss snaps sarcastically.
"No, Claude's our new cleaner. Hell of a nice bloke. He suggested I talk to AI about my contract and everything."
"And?"
"Oh. It agrees with Claude. Oh, and it pointed out that apparently you owe Stephen and me a landline, a 2400 baud modem and a VT100 terminal."
"And I take it that's Stephen's opinion as well?"
"I'm not sure. I'll know when he gets back from gastroenteritis tomorrow. Honestly, that guy needs to use a fridge..."

9630fccb0f6dca09: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — Navigation app Waze rejected on Friday Malaysia’s allegations that it could exploit users’ personal data, after the country banned civil servants from using the app over its Israeli links.

Muslim-majority Malaysia is a longstanding and vocal critic of Israel and maintains no diplomatic relations with it.
Waze, owned by Google, was founded in Israel and remains incorporated there.

“Our decision is not controversial,” the Malaysian leader said, adding that Malaysia was “being monitored” because of its opposition to Israel.
“They will use all their influence to go against us,” Anwar said, calling the issue “a matter of national security”.
Malaysia’s Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo told parliament on Thursday that the ban applied only to civil servants carrying out official duties.
He cited data security and legal concerns for the move, as “user data falls under Israeli jurisdiction”.
The government did not provide further details on the reason for the ban or how it would be enforced or monitored.
Malaysia’s National Security Council warned on Thursday that civil servants who defy the immediate ban “could face disciplinary action”.

Anwar suggested on Wednesday that users of Waze — which uses driver data to provide real-time traffic information — switch to platforms such as TuJu, a locally developed Malaysian road navigation app.
Waze is widely used in Malaysia, including as a back-up navigation aid by drivers for its Grab online cab-hailing service.

Public subscriptions for the IPO crossed 10 times the shares on offer by Friday, driven by strong demand from institutional and retail investors, employees and shareholders. Assuming bids were largely placed at the top end of the 1,119-rupee price band, total demand has now exceeded US$24.5 billion.

That's on top of so-called anchor investors like the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, BlackRock and Fidelity that bid for their exclusively reserved quota on Monday. Their reserved US$854 million worth of shares received bids of over $25 billion.
"This is a Reliance IPO after a long time, which is triggering a lot of exuberance and euphoria for the stock," said Kranthi Bathini, equity strategist at WealthMills Securities.

The IPO values Jio Platforms at up to US$108.3 billion, potentially making it one of India's biggest companies by market capitalisation when trading starts ​on Oct 28. It counts Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google among its investors, and is led by Ambani's eldest son, Akash Ambani.
The IPO got off to an unusually rapid start on Wednesday when the offering was fully subscribed within two hours of opening.
That contrasts with most Indian IPOs, where books typically build gradually and institutional investors often wait until the final hours to place bids.

Jio is part of Ambani's Reliance Industries, a company often seen by Indian investors as a long-term wealth generator. Reliance shares have returned around 900% since 2006, beating the benchmark Nifty index's 685% return, LSEG data shows.

Jio's telecoms business was launched in 2016 and disrupted the market by offering free voice and data, hitting rivals Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea. Today, on the ​basis of customers in a single country, Jio's 500 million-plus users are second only to China Mobile's 600941.SS.

As of Friday, the institutional portion of the IPO was subscribed 26.5 times, underscoring strong demand from large investors. The retail tranche was covered 2.3 times, while bids for the employee and existing Reliance shareholder quotas reached 2.7 and 6.6 times the shares on offer, respectively, exchange data showed.

Reliance was founded by Dhirubhai Ambani, Akash Ambani's grandfather, who cultivated a vast retail investor base through mass shareholder gatherings in Mumbai in the 1980s. On its website, the conglomerate says its 1977 listing helped popularise equity investing in India, "ushering the equity cult" in the country.

76d3b83cc6245b7c: PETALING JAYA: Malaysian households spent more on eating out than on food consumed at home in 2024, averaging RM902.70 a month on meals outside compared with RM875.80 on food at home, Khazanah Research Institute says.
KRI's The State of Households 2026 said the trend came amid growing concerns over the nation's health, with more than half of Malaysian adults classified as overweight or obese in 2023.

Household spending on eating out increased across all income groups between 2019 and 2024, it said, but the rise was more pronounced among the bottom 80% of households, whose average expenditure grew nearly 1.5 times over the five-year period.
For the top 20% of households, spending on eating out increased by less than 1.3 times.
“Possible explanations for this continued increase in eating out expenditure may be both higher living costs and evolving lifestyle behaviours,” the report said.
“These may have implications for public health outcomes as eating out has been linked to poor diet quality, which in turn raises the risk of obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs).”
The report also said the share of the population considered overweight and obese, which are key risks for NCDs, rose between 2019 and 2023.
In 2023, 32.6% of Malaysian adults were overweight and 21.8% were obese, meaning more than half the adult population (54.4%) was above a healthy weight range.

The report also highlighted other worrying health trends, including declining physical activity between 2019 and 2023, particularly in urban areas, where occupations, transport choices, lifestyles and living environments may influence activity levels.
A large proportion of Malaysians also failed to meet recommended fruit and vegetable intake levels in 2023, it said.
Meanwhile, diabetes emerged as one of the five leading causes of death in most states between 2022 and 2024.
