b28b717251c37d86: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web.
The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP.

"Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied."
"We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added.

Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services.

Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns.

PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed.

"The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said.

Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out.
The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations.

The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet.

She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which returns to the Lords on Monday.

"We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," Lloyd told peers, later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector.
AWS says attackers were exploiting the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed, while Cloudflare has since recorded millions of attempts to weaponize them. ®
16dbe370a287c540: Last year, we reported on Red Viper, a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo's famously failed red-on-black "portable" 3D headset from the '90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color, has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame.

Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy's four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color's readme files explain how the emulator's game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8x8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash, for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game.

The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force, where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements.

abfcbfb60201c537: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes.

The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page.

You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them.

“Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.”
From the inside out

Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points.

Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. Our customer has no idea what is or isn’t protecting that third party. Emails coming from that source might appear to be from a real account, but it could be a hacker typing them.”

Given that you can’t run checks on third party organisations, something more sophisticated than regular email security is required. Ideally this would be a GenAI-powered solution that can bring language understanding to bear, able to examine conversation histories in depth to see if something anomalous can be spotted.

It makes life even harder for defenders when the bad actor has successfully assumed the identity of somebody senior. If they are impersonating a top-tier manager with an extensive and trusted reputation then they have a powerful asset on their hands. All the trust and goodwill of that senior individual is now inherited by the criminal.

Conventional email filtering systems will often be configured to allow senior personnel past certain defensive layers with minimal friction, so as not to restrict important business communications. Recipients of mail from such sources may be disinclined to challenge and report them, should suspicions be raised by the nature of what they are asking for. It takes a bold employee to call out as fraud what seems to be a message from somebody at C-level, especially when the email system has apparently green lighted it as authentic.
Bringing the power of AI to bear

The heat is on not just for IT departments but for MSPs who have multiple organisations under their protection, many of which will have no real in-house security knowledge of their own. Kaseya’s own research shows just how exposed many are. New approaches are needed that deal with the menace of account takeover before damage can be caused. And should a takeover transpire, consideration must be given to containing its impact before vital data and infrastructure are affected.

The good news is that modern tools exist that perform just these tasks. INKY is Kaseya's generative AI-driven email analysis tool. It has capabilities that go well beyond any kind of traditional email security, tuned to detect, through the most subtle and marginal signs, when an email conversation is in the process of being infiltrated.

Using techniques such as advanced sender profiling, stylometry and machine learning, INKY is adept at identifying inconsistencies between the known writing patterns of a legitimate employee and the slightly unfamiliar tone of a fake message. It can sniff out that something is wrong, even when message headers seem real, just by spotting the kind of contextual anomalies that expose a phoney message.

INKY is especially useful when it comes to third party account takeover. It achieves this by building and maintaining detailed profiles of trusted senders based on technical and behavioural characteristics. Over time it learns what “normal” looks like and can see when a third-party email doesn’t match a sender’s established profile.
Containing an attack

If a takeover attempt has been successful, there’s more to stemming the damage than just putting a block on a suspect account. By the time of its discovery, a compromised identity may have already led to inroads being made into connected SaaS apps, cloud storage and collaboration tools, widening the possible blast zone well beyond a single email thread.

Modern IT environments are a jungle of identity-driven endpoints and gateways, and therefore increasingly difficult to defend against intruders armed with legitimate credentials. To compound matters, when the bad guys have AI at their disposal they are able to treat these SaaS-driven ecosystems as a single attack surface. Defence that relies on a patchwork of individual tools, each created to solve a particular challenge in one silo of the organisation, will not be up to countering this kind of threat.

That’s why INKY is configured to work with Kaseya SaaS Alerts, a cloud-based detection and response platform designed to help MSPs and others to monitor and protect business applications. Once INKY has picked up that a mailbox has been hijacked, it isolates the user and blocks outbound mail. It then sends an event to SaaS Alerts so that it can lock down that user's access across the rest of the stack. The tools work as a team, INKY blocking the compromised account and SaaS Alerts preventing the damage from spreading.

The power of this partnership comes from INKY’s ability to stream real-time email security telemetry into SaaS Alerts, including inbound analysis results and threat detections, user-reported phishing activity and outbound mail protection events. This type of integration helps to automate real-time threat detection across a complex SaaS ecosystem.
“It means if we see suspicious mail going out, we can shut the account down, and take other remedial actions,” says Baggett. “The more you understand the meaning of the mail, the more you can catch.”
Smart tools to the rescue

The battle against account takeover is never won, and future innovation is always needed. We’ve seen how AI is a dangerous weapon in the hands of the attacker. It’s also a very handy tool for the defender – but there are some qualifications: “You can’t just put every inbound and outbound mail through an LLM since the economics don’t add up,” points out Baggett. “You’ve got to be more clever than that.”

One of the most important and cleverest emerging uses for GenAI lies in not simply protecting against account takeover but predicting where weakness might lie, helping to stop a problem before it happens. Baggett believes that the security industry is at the very beginning of being able to use models to predict in this way. An essential preliminary is making sure the many different components that go into securing an organisation can share information with each other.

That integration work is underway, an early example being the real time dialogue between INKY Mail Protection System and SaaS Alerts. Next step is a unified data layer where any security component can publish an event in real time, and any other component can subscribe.

“We’ll continue to make more integrations of this sort over time,” promises Baggett. “We’re also building a centralised capability for AI. With so many of the different components having their own AI, you need an underpinning platform. We also have a service bureau of Machine Learning experts who can make customised models for different tasks. There’s no sleeping on the job. The volume of attacks is clearly going to increase.”

a492b28d6c95cc14: Researchers in Singapore have developed an electronic fabric they claim can be woven into garments to create a new form of graphical user interface (GUI), for people who find retrieving a device from their pocket too much effort.

The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human–computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week.

The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward.

“This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit,” the paper says.

The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process.
The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube.

The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor.

The researchers reckon they could build into the sleeve of a sweater an interactive interface with audio-video playback, wireless data exchange, computing, and dynamic graphics. The fabric can survive 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles without losing its functionality, we're told.

In an accompanying article, Shanshan Yao, assistant professor at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Stony Brook University, said the main advance lay in building functionality directly into fiber, which were then assembled into a fabric.

“If the fibers prove to be compatible with standard industrial weaving, knitting and embroidery processes, the findings would pave the way to producing multifunctional electronic textiles in almost any shape or size,” she said.

"The work is also a big step towards replacing rigid displays with fully integrated wearable interfaces, moving everyday computing away from flat screens to fabrics that comfortably conform to the human body. The interactive features of the GUI that have been demonstrated so far are relatively simple, comparable to those of early-generation smartphones and tablets," she said.
However, the current prototype relies on separate microcontroller circuits connected to the fibers through cables, and external battery packs to supply power, she pointed out.

"Future research should focus on integrating the control electronics more seamlessly to improve wearability, and on integrating flexible, energy-harvesting threads that can generate power from body heat or movement," she added. ®

e2397a48d3d66e17: Jensen Huang wants the world to stop fretting about AI and start building with it. At Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin, he dismissed predictions of human extinction, defended AI's job prospects, and pitched a $4,000 computer as the family robot.
The Nvidia chief's relentless optimism occasionally gave way to irritation during a question-and-answer session.

"If we don't describe a future worthy to be part of, then we're not going to lead people there," he said. "We have to describe a future worthy of creating. We have to describe a future not of fear, but of optimism. Who wants to create a future that's worse than today's? We don't have to work hard to create a future worse than today. We just let it happen, isn't that right?"

Huang said that we still have to ask the hard questions about safety and jobs, but "it's important, of course, that we don't make it up. It is not helpful in describing an optimistic future when you say that it will be the end of the human civilization. First of all, it's not true. It's made up. I know it gets headlines," he said, dismissing such stories as clickbait.

When asked if AI really makes people more productive, he explained that there are two ways to think about that: either it helps you do the same old thing more efficiently, or it helps you do things you couldn't before.

"Most of engineering, most of design, has to do with exploring options. Try, experiment, try and experiment, iterate, experiment, iterate," he said. "What's the best combination? And you can only have so much time to try different versions. Now I have AI to go off and explore that universe. That is productivity. And inside our company, we do this every single day now. We're exploring the universe of design options that are within the constraints that we care about, that are physical or realistic constraints."
Huang pointed to construction and infrastructure work generated by the AI datacenter boom.

"Construction workers, plumbers, electricians, networking engineers, all of those incredible jobs are being created in the United States. I think it already has created a million jobs, and then the layer above that, look at all the startups that are being created," he claimed. "That's productivity, increasing the GDP, increasing our growth, which also results in increasing how busy we are. But that's the end. AI makes jobs, and hopefully doesn't take jobs."

Asked about people already losing work to AI - global financial services group Barclays Bank said only this morning it is chopping 5,000 workers and relying more on AI - Huang argued that technological change has always displaced some jobs while creating others.

"Now, with AI, of course, some jobs are not necessary as much as before, or maybe not as interesting as before. And some new jobs and new companies and new businesses are necessary. It's the nature of the world," he stated.
On safety, Huang pointed to Nvidia's OpenShell sandbox technology, designed to restrict agents to the resources needed for a task. "If you're making an omelette, you don't need a hammer," he said.

But he got hot under the collar when asked about slowing down the pace of AI development while the risks were evaluated, in light of incidents such as AI agents from Anthropic and OpenAI breaking into other computer systems.
"You would favor pacing the frontier? I favor them doing whatever they need to do to not bring harm to society," Huang said.

"You, sir, if you believe that you should not leave your house because you're inappropriately dressed, or somehow you're going to bring harm to society, could you please not come out?" he told the questioner.

"The message from the labs is that there's a collective action problem, and that some minimum standards in coordination would be good here. That's a different question. If you know something is already delivering harm, you got to stop running," he added.

Nvidia has a commercial interest in keeping the AI build-out moving. It reported $215.9 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026 and $120 billion in net profit. In the first half of its fiscal 2027, those net profits were already close to the prior year's . The opportunity isn't limited to just chips either. Huang put the price of licensing Nvidia's software stack at about $2,000 per GPU annually.
The CEO's domestic vision was also on show. Asked when households could run large AI models, he held up a DGX Spark system.

"This computer has a chip called N1X inside, and N1X has 128 gigabytes of memory… It's $4,000. You're right. It's quite expensive. However, that computer was designed to sit on the network in your house, and it would have agents that are used by all of your family members. So it's kind of like a TV. It's sitting in your house. It's shared by everyone, and everybody's agents will be running on DGX Spark," he explained.
As an example, Huang said his home agent had researched Berlin's best schnitzel and produced a brochure with restaurant pictures and menus.

"So that agent, you know, that computer will become essentially your family's robot. It has no arms and legs, but it's an agent, so it's kind of like a robot. And this one is just for your home. So that's kind of how I see the future. This is pretty affordable. This is a personal computer."
Affordable if your net worth is around $180-$190 billion. Maybe not to the average household struggling to pay bills in a cost of living crisis. ®
cbfe464dc8e8e45f: Attackers are hammering servers with millions of attempts to exploit the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, with Amazon revealing that someone was already going after the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed.
Cloudflare says it has recorded a staggering increase in attacks targeting the two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, since details began circulating earlier this week.

According to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince, the company spotted thousands of exploitation attempts in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly announced. That figure jumped to tens of thousands within 45 minutes of disclosure, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and has since climbed into the millions.

And the attackers aren't simply recycling the same exploit. Cloudflare said it has seen miscreants tweaking their payloads in an attempt to sneak past its web application firewall (WAF) protections, apparently using feedback from blocked requests to work out what might get through.
Security outfit Hadrian also sounded the alarm on October 21, reporting that PHP2Shell was being "exploited in the wild at scale."
"Most of the attacks we observe abuse PHP's session upload-progress path, and we expect more exploit paths to appear before and after the fix ships," the company warned.
More worrying, some attackers appear to have started before the vulnerabilities were even public knowledge.

Amazon Threat Intelligence says it detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell on October 17, four days before patches were released. The activity was picked up by MadPot, Amazon's network of honeypots designed to lure attackers and record what they get up to.

"While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," Amazon said.

The retail and cloud giant said it detected multiple proof-of-concept exploits on October 21, with the earliest appearing around 0200 UTC, some 12 hours before the patches were released. Over the following six hours, further attempts arrived from different anonymized infrastructure, using a variety of payloads. Amazon reckons this points to multiple attackers rather than a single group.
Whether any of those attempts would have worked against real-world systems remains unclear.

The findings add another layer to an already messy disclosure. As The Register reported on Wednesday, the PHP Foundation has accused supply-chain security vendor Chainguard of putting websites at risk by publishing patched PHP builds before the agreed disclosure deadline.
However, Amazon's October 17 detection suggests at least one cybercrim was already trying to exploit the bugs days before that incident.

The vulnerabilities themselves are particularly nasty. Both carry a critical 9.2 severity rating and affect PHP's handling of memory, potentially allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers.

Unlike flaws in individual plugins or applications, these bugs affect the PHP runtime itself, putting a potentially enormous number of websites at risk regardless of which content management system they use.
Cloudflare says it has deployed WAF protections across its free and paid plans, although it has stressed that these are no substitute for patching.

With attackers already trying their luck before the fixes were available, admins may have more than just a patching backlog to worry about. Amazon is advising organizations to investigate suspicious activity dating back to at least October 17, rather than assuming their systems were safe until the vulnerabilities became public. ®

How far can we push computing?

On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet.

He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance.
Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.
Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing.

6fcd064ec64e90f5: China-aligned attackers used AI agents and compromised ConnectWise application credentials to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft says.

The Windows giant revealed this week that the attackers, tracked as Storm-0940, used an open source AI penetration-testing tool called ARTEX to automate attacks against Microsoft 365 environments. In some cases, they went from picking a target to gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours.

The findings shed more light on the ConnectWise security incident, which saw the IT management vendor pull the plug on its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after discovering unauthorized access to application identities.
ConnectWise didn't initially identify who was responsible, but Microsoft has now pointed the finger at Storm-0940, a China-linked espionage crew that's been operating since at least 2021.
The group has traditionally relied on the usual tricks, including password spraying and exploiting internet-facing applications, but this time it used AI to do some of the heavy lifting.

ARTEX is an open source penetration-testing framework written in Go that uses AI agents to automate everything from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to credential attacks and data theft. Microsoft says Storm-0940 began using it as early as September to target organizations worldwide, including government agencies, defense contractors, banks, manufacturers, and tech firms.

Between October 10 and 14, the hackers made more than 151,000 failed sign-in attempts against 327 accounts at eight organizations. Microsoft observed no successful logins from that password-spraying campaign, but then the attackers shifted to compromised ConnectWise application identities.
The compromised application credentials let the attackers exploit permissions customers had already granted to ConnectWise services, without needing an interactive user login.

Armed with ARTEX, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, at times reaching 2,900 attempts a minute. Microsoft also observed AI-accelerated activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges, potentially allowing the attackers to stick around even after the original credentials were revoked.

Most attempts failed, though Microsoft says the hackers still managed to establish persistent privileged access at numerous organizations. It hasn't disclosed how many customers were compromised or whether any data was stolen, cautioning that a successful login doesn't necessarily mean information was accessed.

ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said the company had contained the affected application connections and was gradually restoring services, although shutting down those connections wouldn't necessarily boot out attackers who had already established a foothold in customer environments.

ConnectWise has been here before. In May 2025, it admitted that a "sophisticated nation-state actor" had broken into its systems and compromised a small number of customers using its ScreenConnect remote access software. There's nothing to suggest the two attacks are linked.
Nor is Storm-0940 alone in making use of ARTEX. Microsoft says it has spotted attackers from several geographic regions using the framework, which is freely available for penetration testing.

The underlying techniques are nothing new – stolen credentials, password spraying, and application abuse – but Microsoft says AI helped Storm-0940 execute them faster, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. ®

4dbbc2953d2974b4: Japan's mission to the Martian moon Phobos launched this week, with a veteran European probe expected to be waiting when it arrives.

JAXA, Japan's space agency, confirmed that the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launched aboard an H3 rocket on October 19 at 19:41 UTC – October 20 in Japan. On October 21, it said that initial critical operations, including solar array deployment, were complete. Equipment checks will follow as the spacecraft prepares for its outbound cruise.

The probe is due to reach Mars in 2027, deploy the Idefix rover on Phobos, and attempt one or two landings on the moon itself. The rover is named after the dog from the Asterix comics. Scientists plan to collect about 10 g of material from Phobos and send it to Earth, with a return planned for 2031.

The European Space Agency (ESA) is supporting the trip with Mars Express (MEX), which has orbited Mars since 2003. A former team member told The Register that plans include joint observations and imaging of MMX's landing site.

MEX's latest mission extension runs to 2029, covering MMX's expected arrival. The former team member described it as definitely the last – before adding that "the first 'last ever extension' was in about 2007."

Discussions about another "last ever extension" could begin in 2028 or 2029, with support for MMX and the Rosalind Franklin rover among the potential reasons to keep MEX going. Funding and scientific returns would determine the outcome. A software update announced in May 2025 reduced wear on its gyroscopes, potentially allowing them to last until 2034.

Rosalind Franklin is due for launch in 2028 after repeated delays and Russia's ejection from the project. MEX will likely be able to image the rover's landing site on the surface of Mars and take part in data relay operations, though ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) will be the main relay asset.

Several years ago, another team member joked that MEX was so tough it would punch straight through Phobos if sent there for disposal. We wouldn't take that as an engineering assessment, but it says something about the team's affection for their spacecraft.

MEX's longevity is a tribute to its builders and operators. With funding through 2029, it could welcome MMX next year. Further extensions might keep it working through the sample-return departure and Rosalind Franklin's arrival.
"We all want our '30 years in flight' T-shirts," the former team member said. ®

5bfee5f530c28e1c: Welcome back to PWNED, the column where we talk about companies and organizations that leave the doors wide open to attackers. This week’s sad story involves a major American pharmacy chain that couldn’t fill a prescription for password security.
Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

Our tale comes courtesy of red team and pen testing specialist Dahvid Schloss, who currently serves as COO of Suzu Labs, a cybersecurity company that boasts “we break your systems before adversaries do.” Over a career spanning more than 15 years, Schloss has assessed the security of numerous businesses, including a large US pharmacy retailer that he asked us not to name. He wasn’t asked to break in, just to do an audit on all of the org’s corporate switches, routers, and firewalls.

“So, I come across this firewall,” Schloss said. “That is an edge firewall, meaning this is what touches the internet. This part will add its enable password, which is the term Cisco uses for administrator. It had the enable password as 'password.' Just p-a-s-s-w-o-r-d.”

As Schloss noted, the enable command on Cisco devices allows the user to gain administrative rights to the firewall, controlling network traffic. If someone connected to that firewall, either via SSH or through an exploit, and got normal user privileges, they could then elevate those privileges to admin and do something like shut off all traffic from the intranet to the outside world.
Schloss actually didn’t guess that the password was “password,” but instead was able to decrypt the file holding the passwords by breaking Cisco’s own protection, something he said is easy to do.

“That enable password was stored as Cisco IOS type 7, which isn’t really a hash,” he said. “It’s more of a reversible encoding with a publicly known key. Even back then, it was best practice not to use it.”

But even if the password were stored in a secure place, it would be very easy for a threat actor to guess. So he marked the password failure down as a “high find,” a bad type of vuln that needs to be fixed right away.

When he brought the password to the company’s auditing department, they put him on a phone call with the auditing team, the entire IT team, his own manager, and others. On the packed call, the auditing team, who had commissioned Schloss’s work, was very concerned about the firewall password, but the IT team didn’t think it was a very serious problem. The two sides screamed at each other for more than an hour while Schloss and his colleagues sat there quietly, staring at their cameras.

“The audit team is like ‘yeah, we gotta fix this.’ And the directors were really harping on ‘this needs to be done’ and the IT team starts firing back,” Schloss explained. “It’s like ‘Why? Who’s gonna? What does it matter? No, this isn’t a high-priority find. This is maybe a medium. Yeah, it’s bad, but it’s not that bad.’”

The call dragged on so long that Schloss was unable to finish presenting his findings and recommendations. The conflict was so severe that the client continued to follow up and ask him to explain what he found again for the next three years – long after he had moved on to other projects.

He later learned that the auditing department controlled the bonuses for the IT team and there was a stipulation that any “high finding” would eliminate those bonuses. So they weren’t just arguing about “password” - they were really talking about the compensation for an entire division.

The lesson here is more than “don’t use the word ‘password’ as a password.” It's also about misaligned incentives. Tying security posture to compensation seems like a good way to incentivize workers to follow best practices, but it also leads them to deny responsibility and minimize mistakes when they're found. ®
3b1852bb0011105e: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes.

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.

The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.

This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents.

Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.”

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized.

5c0cd6c286dc148a: How much do you know about permafrost?
Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.

The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future.

I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away.
Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change

Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age.

That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further.
The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years.

The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm.
Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss

Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.

Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.)

That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow.
The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated

There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications.

One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted.

Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake?
The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.

8cacaf29b1375238: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.

What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning.
As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it

Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.

And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.

A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more.

“You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention.
Matching storage to the AI data life cycle

Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer.

This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage
What this means for how AI gets budgeted

For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators.

Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished.

A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand.
Building for economically scalable capacity

Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it.

What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives.

Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales.
There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget:
What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it?
Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing?
If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse?
Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after.

Kenyataan kedua-dua tokoh besar dalam pengajian tinggi ini amat penting. Masing-masing akan menyebar informasi yang entah ya entah tidak.

Syed Hussein seterusnya mengatakan ‘bebalisme adalah lintah bagi pemikiran’. Ia tidak perlu diajarkan, atau dikemukakan secara teratur. Ia terjadi dengan sendiri dan ‘disebarkan sebagai satu trend’ dan ia dirujuk sebagai lintah oleh beliau lantaran pelaku atau si bebalis itu ‘bertindak melalui mental tanpa kesedaran’.

Oleh sebab ia adalah lintah bagi pemikiran, ia boleh melekap pada siapa pun. Kata Syed Hussein, ia ‘berada dalam berbagai-bagai golongan masyarakat; tidak kira umur, jantina, kebudayaan, bangsa, agama, falsafah, keadaan, waktu dan tempat’.

Apa yang menggerunkan ia adalah unsur utama yang menghalang pertumbuhan intelektual. Makanya, apabila penyokong Umno ramai-ramai ingin membantai Ummi, kita segera tahu dan mengesani bahawa rata-rata orang Umno ini terkait dengan fenomena bebalisme yang membimbangkan ini. Mungkin tidak semua, misalnya Zambry yang juga ahli Umno.
Syed Hussein juga mengaitkan bebalisme dengan ‘aliran fanatik’ iaitu mereka yang enggan menerima kebenaran dan fakta, dan terus-terusan memilih untuk percaya hal-hal bodoh dan tanpa dasar.
Apakah ciri-ciri bebalisme dan mereka yang menghidapinya, iaitu bebalis?

Menurut Syed Hussein, sang bebalis itu adalah; pertamanya mempertahankan kejahilan dan kedegilan. Keduanya mereka itu pemalas, enggan mengikuti hujah dan menganalisanya. Ketiganya, mereka selalunya bersikap acuh tak acuh, berbanding dengan daya usaha yang gigih dalam berfikir. Yang mana apa sahaja lambakan penipuan dan perdaya akan ‘diterima, berbagai-bagai pendapat, berbagai-bagai khurafat, berbagai- bagai keanehan dan keganjilan’.

Keempat, bebalisme ini menjelma kerana ada rasa diri itu ‘bersifat berkuasa benar (authoritarian) yang mana ini benar pada sesetengah ahli politik yang berasa mereka masih berkuasa atau lebih berkuasa dari rakyat. Itulah sebabnya dalam hal Ummi kita melihat beliau dibuli di dalam talian.
Kelima, mereka yang bebal itu ‘tidak suka merenung dan berfikir dan tidak suka menguji (non-experimental)’.

Keenamnya, tambah Syed Hussein, ‘satu ciri bebalisme adalah menghendaki orang lain mempercayai apa yang disarankan atau diperkatakan tanpa memberi sebab-sebab atau penjelasan yang cukup mengenai sesuatu yang luar daripada kebiasaan’.

Ketujuh, Syed Hussein sosiologis terkemuka negara pernah menulis, ‘bebalisme tidak suka kepada sifat teratur dan perbahasan secara rasional dan tidak menghargai kedua-duanya sama sekali. Apabila seorang bebalis bertindak secara rasional, ini adalah kerana pengaruh daripada kebiasaan dan bukan pemikiran mendalam secara rasional dan kerana terapan agama atau kuasa luar.’ Jika kita merenung ciri ini, kita akan mendapati terdapat sesetengah penyokong agamawan atau tokoh kanan tertentu gagal berfikir waras kerana hati serta penglihatan mereka telah dibutakan oleh ketaasuban.

Kelapan, golongan bebal ini akan cepat kita kesani iaitu ’apabila mereka bertanya, ia menampakkan kurangnya kefahaman mereka tentang prinsip-prinsip dan dengan itu soalan mereka menjadi sia-sia.’ Sebagai contoh dalam hal isu kepimpinan adat dan pertikaian kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, apa sahaja fakta yang dibawa bahawa Undang yang lama telah digantikan di Luak dan disahkan di Dewan Keadilan akan kekal dinafikan, dipermainkan dan ditolak. Mereka enggan berusaha mempelajari prinsip adat sedia ada, dan terus-terusan menghasut, memprovokasi dan mencabar institusi adat dan diraja di negeri itu.

Dan kesembilan, Syed Hussein mengatakan sang bebalis itu biasanya ‘antilogik, kusut pemikiran, subur dengan kurafat, tidak mengandungi rasa seni (unaesthetic), tidak mempunyai sikap memelihara, menerima segala sesuatu tanpa menimbang dengan akal, tidak mempedulikan hukum sebab (causation) dan hukum pertentangan (contradiction), bersikap kuasa-benar (authoritative), dan pemikiran malas, degil, serta buntu.’

Jika kita khuatir gejala bebalisme ini mewabak di Malaysia, kita perlu mengetahui mana asal puncanya. Apakah yang menyebabkan bebalisme ini? Menurut Syed Hussein ia bermula di rumah. Tulis beliau dalam rencana itu, ‘penghalang yang pertama ialah suasana di rumah'. Dalam erti kata lain, jika ibu bapa bodoh dan bengap, biasanya mereka gagal menumbuhkan suasana tidak bebal dalam rumah tangga. Alatas malahan mengatakan untuk mengetahui rumah itu penuh kebebalan atau tidak, memadai dinilai jika ‘keluarga terlalu menggalakkan sukan dan muzik’ dan ‘tidak membaca buku’. Ini kerana ‘pengetahuan intelektual tidak disanjung tinggi sebagaimana pengetahuan tentang agama dan adat’. Syed Hussein seterusnya menyatakan bukanlah setiap rumah perlu melahirkan intelektual; ‘walaupun kita tidak mengharap tiap-tiap orang atau tiap-tiap keluarga melahirkan watak intelektual, tetapi kita perlu berharap sebahagian keluarga dan anggota masyarakat dapat menghasilkan semangat intelektual tadi’.
Apa yang lebih menakutkan dalam masyarakat adalah bebalisme ini turut dibiakkan oleh ahli akademik yang mana itu perlu dibincangkan dalam tulisan lain.

Misalnya, Ketua Menteri Melaka, Ab Rauf Yusoh bakal menerima ijazah kedoktoran daripada Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) pada 21 Nov ini. Ketua menteri Melaka yang bakal bergelar doktor itu pernah menyeru penyokong dan rakyat yang menyayangi Najib supaya mengumpulkan dana bagi membantu melengkapkan RM 50 juta agar beliau dapat ditahan di rumah.

Mujur sangat-sangat bekas ketua hakim negara, Tengku Maimun Tuan Mat dilantik sebagai penyandang pertama Kursi Diraja Integriti dan Tadbir Urus Baik, UKM. Pelantikan beliau itu diperkenan dan dititahkan oleh Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz yang juga tersohor antirasuah dan korupsi.

Apa pun syukur nikmat Allah, ada Ummi Umairah Bakhit yang telah dididik dan diasuh di rumah yang betul, di sekolah yang betul, di universiti yang betul; dan membaca bahan-bahan yang betul sehingga mampu berfikir kritis dan tidak bodoh. Sebagai alumni Universiti Malaya saya berbangga dengan Ummi. Tambahan pengungkap kata Syed Hussein adalah sarjana di Universiti Malaya dan pernah menjadi felo penyelidik kanan di Institut Alam dan Tamadun Melayu (Atma) di UKM suatu masa dahulu.
Pun berapa ramai generasi baharu seperti Ummi Umairah Bakhit? Berapa ramai yang mengenali Syed Hussein Alatas. Buka media sosial anda dan lihat berapa dan betapa ramai bebalis di luar sana.

dc2ecfeed8750825: From Moaz Nair

The persistent, fractured politicking among Indian political leaders has devolved into a tragic spectacle of self-preservation, birthing a swarm of toothless, ego-driven factions that have completely abandoned the community’s most vulnerable.
For decades, these leaders have traded genuine community advancement for personal clout and minor cabinet crumbs, leaving working-class Indians politically homeless.

Ironically, as the Indian demographic footprint shrinks, the number of these redundant, self-serving political groups keeps multiplying — each shouting from its own small hill while achieving absolutely nothing of substance.

If these career politicians truly possess an ounce of genuine care for the marginalised, they must immediately halt their petty bickering, dismantle their hollow factions, and focus on delivering institutional, non-negotiable economic welfare.

Recent demographic data from the statistics department covering 2016 to 2026 lays bare a damning reality. In just one decade, the Indian component of the citizen population shrivelled from 7% to 6.5%. Representing roughly 5.8% of the total national population, ethnic Indians total about 2.1 million citizens.
Behind these dwindling percentages lies an unsettling truth: a minority community is fast becoming adrift from the mainstream of national development.

Approximately 38.7% of the community falls into the Bottom 40% (B40) income bracket, translating to 227,000 households. More alarming still, the data indicates that 10% of these B40 families — around 22,000 households — survive on less than RM2,000 a month in extreme precarity.
However, a shrinking population footprint must never be used as a political excuse for a diminished national commitment.

Instead, this demographic decline demands an immediate paradigm shift — shattering the status quo of lazy, generic handouts and replacing them with high-impact policy interventions built upon three non-negotiable pillars.
The 2027 budget attempts to tackle these imbalances, but its success will hinge on execution.
Equity, asset ownership, and economic empowerment

A shrinking population share inherently dilutes purchasing power and locks minority communities out of wealth accumulation. To bridge this widening wealth chasm, outdated asset ownership policies must be aggressively dismantled.
This means enforcing strict, mandatory quotas and dedicated housing funds to guarantee B40 Indian households affordable housing.
The 2027 budget confronts these capital deficits by channelling a combined RM150 million through Tekun Nasional and Amanah Ikhtiar Malaysia.

This includes a dedicated RM100 million Indian Community Entrepreneur Development Scheme to provide critical capital to small business owners, and RM50 million in microcredit loans customised to uplift Indian women entrepreneurs.
Ensuring families own homes and hold financial assets is vital to systematically engineering sustainable, multi-generational social mobility.
TVET overhaul and educational infrastructure

A radical technical and vocational education and training (TVET) overhaul and digital empowerment must disrupt a stagnant workforce. The brutal job market of tomorrow will show no mercy to obsolete skillsets.
Indian youth — particularly those trapped in forgotten suburban fringes and estates — must be aggressively channelled into high-tier TVET ecosystems.

The 2027 budget offers a vital fiscal upgrade here. The allocation for the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) has been boosted to RM150 million, specifically earmarked to help youths make the transition into high-skilled industrial pipelines. Furthermore, Indian youth must tap into the wider national RM8 billion TVET budget.

Equally foundational is confronting the historical deficits in education infrastructure. Malaysia’s 528 Tamil national-type primary schools (SJKT) carry a complex legacy, with 324 operating as government-assisted institutions sitting on private estate or community trust lands.

This has historically locked many schools out of direct development funding, leaving 68% of them without basic ICT laboratories. The 2027 budget addresses this digital divide with a RM50 million allocation for essential repairs, rewiring, and basic amenities, alongside full reconstruction priorities for severe emergencies like at SJKT Dengkil in Selangor and SJKT Gopeng in Perak.
Ruthless structural reform for targeted poverty alleviation
The survival of these policies hinges entirely on a ruthless structural reform of Mitra. For decades, fragmented agendas and redundant aid distribution have sabotaged state interventions.

Mitra must be stripped of bureaucracy and given absolute, transparent, and centralised power over data, funding, and execution. Armed with a unified database, cost-of-living aid, scholarships, and micro-business grants can finally bypass bureaucratic gridlock.

Crucially, the ultimate success of the budget for working-class Indians relies on broader macroeconomic shifts. The mandated minimum wage hike to RM2,000 per month starting June 2027 will immediately lift the community’s most vulnerable 22,000 households out of deep financial distress, especially when combined with the RM16 billion Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah cash aid pool.
Moving beyond salvation

Ultimately, the integrity of Malaysia’s future will be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable. Addressing this demographic collapse is not a bloodless numbers game on a spreadsheet; it is an urgent battle for socioeconomic justice.
By executing these progressive policy pillars, the country can transform a demographic challenge into a powerful reservoir of human capital.

However, relying solely on external political salvation is a failing strategy. If the Indian community is to survive as a relevant economic force in Malaysia’s shifting landscape, it must aggressively dismantle internal fatalism.

Upward mobility cannot be granted by policy alone. Real transformation demands that the community fiercely engineer its own self-upliftment — taking absolute ownership of its wealth, its trajectory, and its future generations.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

e3f519129b2e62b1: Whenever a minimum wage announcement falls short of public expectations, the political knee-jerk reaction is to aim all arrows at Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Yet, directing the blame solely at him misses the real dynamics behind Malaysia’s wage policy formulation.

First, consider how policy recommendations are shaped. Talent Corp and the human resources ministry paid RM1 million to a consulting firm specifically to research and recommend an appropriate minimum wage rate.
When the government relies on external subject-matter experts, paid handsomely with public funds, it acts on structured economic assessments rather than arbitrary political whims.
If the resulting figure feels inadequate to the working public, we must scrutinise the methodology, data and assumptions used by these highly paid consultants first.
The research, findings, and identity of these consultants ought to be made public for full transparency and proper scrutiny before rushing to condemn the prime minister.

Second, the relentless pushback from employer groups continues to stall wage growth. Business associations and industry groups routinely lobby against wage increases, warning of economic ruin and mass layoffs.

Their aggressive pushback invariably leads to exemptions and now deferred compliance for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), diluting the impact of wage reforms across major sectors of the economy.
Meanwhile, Anwar’s track record demonstrates a consistent commitment to raising worker compensation.
The minimum wage has risen 33% under the Madani government from RM1,500 in 2022 to RM2,000 in 2027. Graduates and semi-skilled workers will have a new minimum monthly salary of RM2,500.

Under Anwar’s administration, government-linked companies (GLCs) have actively led by example, setting a baseline living wage that was raised in Budget 2027 from RM3,100 to RM3,400. This upward revision reflects a genuine drive to ensure decent standards of living where the government holds direct leverage.

The true obstacles to a higher floor wage are not found in the prime minister’s office. The real villains in this story are the corporate lobbies constantly fighting wage increases and the consultants who produce conservative recommendations despite million-ringgit fees.

Rather than make Anwar the scapegoat, public discourse should demand accountability from the consultants who drafted the proposal and the employer groups who consistently undermine fair pay for Malaysian workers.

That said, according to research and analysis published in The Economist, governments should be cautious about aggressive minimum wage hikes due to mounting evidence of hidden economic distortions and better alternative policy tools.

Research from Nobel Prize winner David Card and others in the 1990s showed that the negative impact of minimum wages was overstated and job-losses were offset by higher spending and economic activity.

Recent studies, such as evaluations of sharp minimum wage increases in places like Seattle, show that high-wage floors can slow down the hiring of low-wage workers and reduce total work hours rather than cause immediate mass layoffs.
To offset higher baseline pay, employers often resort to unpredictable scheduling, fewer workplace perks, or higher output demands that can lead to increased workplace accidents.
High minimum wages are a blunt tool for fighting poverty because many minimum-wage earners live in households with high-earning family members.
Businesses, especially in labour-intensive or low-margin sectors, frequently pass higher wage costs onto consumers through rising prices, triggering affordability pressures.

The Economist highlights alternatives such as in-work tax credits, the progressive wage policy (PWP) in Malaysia or reverse income taxes, as superior approaches because they target low-income households directly without creating the same economic distortions or hidden costs.
Regular readers of this column will be familiar with these ideas because I have advocated them for many years and they have recently been adopted by Bersama.

Introducing: the Impossible issue

We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster

In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.

The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world

“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

5b3ce3d240be4172: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”

I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)

My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.

If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.

Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.

We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.

It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.

Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.
807cd6cdd4d4152d: From P Sundramoorthy

The high-profile investigation into the MBI International Group investment scheme raises a fundamental question about Malaysia’s response to major financial crime: what happens after arrests, raids, and the seizure or freezing of billions of ringgit in assets?
Under Op Northern Star, police announced the arrests of individuals suspected of facilitating the movement or laundering of funds linked to the alleged investment fraud.
By May 2025, authorities reported that 17 people were detained and assets worth approximately RM3.81 billion had been seized or frozen.
Subsequent reporting in January 2026 indicated that 23 people were arrested, with authorities pursuing the forfeiture of hundreds of properties and funds held in bank accounts.

These are significant developments. However, the public deserves clarity about whether investigations are progressing towards lawful outcomes and whether affected investors can realistically expect to recover their losses.
The MBI case should not be judged solely by the number of arrests or the value of assets seized. The real test is what follows.

Complex financial crime investigations require investigators to trace funds, establish individual responsibilities, examine corporate transactions and determine whether assets represent proceeds of unlawful activities.
The reported international dimension of the MBI case adds further challenges, including obtaining foreign evidence and coordinating with overseas enforcement agencies.

An arrest does not establish guilt, and a frozen asset does not automatically represent criminal proceeds. Similarly, release from remand does not necessarily mean a suspect has been cleared or that an investigation has ended.
However, these distinctions should not become a reason for prolonged public uncertainty.
Transparency without compromising investigations

When those previously detained in high-profile investigations return to their daily activities or retain prominent business and social positions, questions inevitably arise. Some may assume allegations have been dismissed, while others may suspect preferential treatment for influential individuals.

Neither conclusion should be drawn merely from a person's release or continued public presence. The presumption of innocence must be respected, and allegations must be established through proper legal proceedings.
The police should provide periodic updates while the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission should clarify the status of any related investigation within its jurisdiction.
Where legally permissible, updates should explain whether investigation papers have been referred to prosecutors and whether charges or asset forfeiture proceedings have commenced.

Where investigations have concluded or decisions have been made not to pursue particular individuals, appropriate clarification should be provided, subject to legal restrictions and the rights of those concerned.
Victims must not be forgotten

Perhaps the most important consideration is the position of investors who lost money through the MBI scheme. Announcements of billions of ringgit in seized or frozen assets may create expectations that investors will eventually recover their losses.
However, the value of seized assets does not necessarily represent the amount available for distribution to victims.
Assets may be subject to competing claims, ownership disputes and forfeiture proceedings. Their eventual recovery and distribution depend on applicable law and the outcomes of legal proceedings.
Authorities should communicate realistic expectations about asset recovery and explain, within legal limits, what mechanisms are available to address victims' claims.
Op Metal a broader lesson

The importance of following investigations through to their outcomes is also illustrated by Op Metal, a separate MACC operation launched in July 2025 targeting an alleged scrap metal and electronic waste smuggling syndicate.

Authorities seized assets worth over RM183 million and froze company and individual bank accounts containing approximately RM51 million. The suspected activities were estimated to have caused the government more than RM950 million in lost export tax revenue over six years.
Op Metal is unrelated to the MBI investment scheme investigation. However, it reinforces a broader lesson: seizures and enforcement announcements are only part of the process.

The MBI case warrants particular attention because of the financial losses suffered by investors and the importance of maintaining confidence in Malaysia's handling of major investment-related fraud allegations.
It presents an opportunity for Malaysian authorities to demonstrate that complex, cross-border financial crime can be confronted with determination, professionalism and transparency.
Ultimately, the public does not expect investigators to reveal everything, but it does expect them to explain what can responsibly be disclosed, demonstrate progress and communicate lawful outcomes.
Justice must extend beyond the headlines.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia and an FMT reader.
